name: Herb vs spice: which part of the plant
scope: The organizing puzzle of the whole spice rack: an 'herb' is a LEAF, a 'spice' is any OTHER part of a plant. T1: the green things you'd grow on a windowsill (basil, mint, oregano, bay) are the LEAVES of a soft plant, and being a leaf is exactly what makes something an herb. T2: cinnamon is not a leaf, seed, or root at all, it is the inner BARK of a tree, peeled and dried until it curls. T3: cloves are a flower part caught before it opened, the dried unopened flower BUD. T4: saffron is a female flower part, the three red STIGMAS plucked from a crocus. T5: ginger and turmeric are not roots, they are underground STEMS (rhizomes) that creep sideways through the soil. T5b (payoff): one nutmeg fruit yields TWO spices from two different parts, the SEED (nutmeg) and the lacy red ARIL around it (mace).
source: Grokipedia attempted this session but blocked (WebFetch 403 / Chrome extension not connected); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Spice', 'Herb', 'Cinnamon', 'Saffron', 'Ginger', 'Rhizome', 'Nutmeg'. Cross-checked against the per-spice ladder sources below.
framing_note: Scene-led: show the spice and ask which PART of the plant it is; never 'what is a spice?'. This is the taxonomy BACKBONE of the sub-strand, so each rung's answer stays on the plant-part fact while the individual-spice ladders carry the STORIES (no same-fact overlap). Accuracy rail: ginger/turmeric are rhizomes (underground STEMS), NOT roots, the classic trap. Dinner-test payoff: the ginger/turmeric 'root that isn't a root' rung.

name: Black pepper: the king-of-spices vine
scope: The world's most-traded spice, and every peppercorn is a tiny dried fruit. T1: a peppercorn is the dried BERRY (a drupe) of a climbing VINE, so pepper grows on a vine, not a bush or tree. T2: that vine is native to the MALABAR COAST of southwest India, the historic heart of the pepper trade. T3: black, green, and white peppercorns all come from the SAME plant, black being the unripe berry cooked and sun-dried until the skin blackens and wrinkles. T4: white pepper is the same berry left to RIPEN, then soaked so the dark outer skin rots away, leaving the pale inner seed (milder, used so black flecks don't show in light sauces). T5: pepper's bite comes from PIPERINE, a completely different molecule from chili's capsaicin, which is why pepper-burn and chili-burn feel different. T6 (history payoff): medieval Europe prized pepper so highly it was counted out almost like money and helped drive the sea route to India (Vasco da Gama). T7 (name origin): the word 'pepper' actually comes from LONG PEPPER (Sanskrit pippali), a hotter relative Europeans knew first, before the name slid onto the round peppercorn.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Black pepper', Britannica 'black-pepper-plant', Farmers' Almanac 'Where Do Peppercorns Come From', McCormick Science Institute 'Black Pepper'.
framing_note: Prep-frame fine ('the pepper you grind'). Invert the wonder: lead with 'most-traded spice / counted like coins', answer is the vine/berry/Malabar. Accuracy rail (hard): pepper's heat is PIPERINE, NOT capsaicin; pepper is an Old-World vine, chili a New-World fruit, keep them separate. Dinner-test payoff: black/white/green are ONE plant at different ripeness+processing (T3/T4). Keep the da Gama rung food-anchored (the pepper is why the voyage happened), never a bare date/agency.

name: Nutmeg, mace and the Spice Islands
scope: Two different spices from one fruit, and a spice people were killed over. T1: crack a nutmeg fruit and you find a hard brown SEED (nutmeg) wrapped in a lacy scarlet net; that dried red net is a SECOND spice called MACE, so one fruit gives two spices. T2: for centuries this tree grew in only ONE place on Earth, the tiny BANDA ISLANDS of eastern Indonesia (the 'Spice Islands'). T3: cloves came from the same neighborhood, the nearby Maluku islands like Ternate and Tidore, making this small archipelago the world's only source of three prized spices. T4 (history payoff): to lock up the nutmeg monopoly, the Dutch East India Company under Jan Pieterszoon Coen seized Banda in 1621 and nearly wiped out its people. T5 (history payoff): in 1667 (Treaty of Breda) the Dutch handed England a nutmeg island called RUN in exchange for keeping New Amsterdam, which England had renamed New York, so Manhattan was effectively swapped for a nutmeg island. T6 (honest fact): nutmeg in large amounts is mildly toxic and intoxicating, which is why a recipe only ever asks for a tiny grating.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands' and 'Nutmeg', Atlas Obscura 'island-traded-for-Manhattan', NBC News 'Why the Banda Islands Were Once More Valuable Than Manhattan'.
framing_note: The FOOD (nutmeg/mace) is ALWAYS the anchor; the wars are told only because the spice caused them, never geopolitics for its own sake. State the Banda killings matter-of-factly and briefly for a kid (people were killed to control the spice), no gore. Accuracy rail: nutmeg and mace are the SEED and its ARIL of the SAME fruit; nutmeg grew only in the Bandas. Dinner-test payoff: Manhattan-for-a-nutmeg-island (Run, 1667), with the answer food-anchored (why the island mattered = nutmeg).

name: Vanilla: the hand-pollinated orchid
scope: The world's second-priciest spice is the cured fruit of an orchid, made affordable by a 12-year-old boy. T1: vanilla is the seed POD ('bean') of an ORCHID, the only orchid grown for food. T2: the orchid is native to MEXICO, where in the wild it is pollinated by one specific local bee (a Melipona) found nowhere else, so vines planted overseas flowered but never set fruit. T3 (history payoff): in 1841 on Reunion, an enslaved boy named EDMOND ALBIUS, age 12, invented a fast hand-pollination trick (lift the flap with a splinter, press the pollen on by hand) that is still used on every vanilla bean today. T4: a fresh green vanilla pod has almost NO flavor or smell; the taste only develops during weeks of sweating and drying (CURING), which builds up the vanillin. T5 (honest fact): most 'vanilla' flavor in cheap food is not from the orchid at all, it is synthetic vanillin made from wood pulp or petrochemicals, because real vanilla is so costly.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Edmond Albius' and 'Vanilla', CBC Ideas 'history-vanilla-slavery' (Eric Jennings lecture), Linnean Society 'Edmond Albius', Nautilus 'The Boy Who Was King of Vanilla'.
framing_note: Lead with the wonder ('second-priciest spice', 'the only orchid we eat'); answer is the orchid/pod/curing. Tell the Albius beat factually and with dignity (enslaved boy, age 12, never credited or paid); it is real history told straight, not a moral quiz, no editorializing. Accuracy rail: the Mexican pollinator is geographically LIMITED (endemic), NOT extinct; vanilla grown abroad simply lacked it until hand-pollination. Dinner-test payoff: the Albius hand-pollination rung (T3).

name: Chili heat, capsaicin and the Scoville scale
scope: Chili 'heat' is a chemical trick, and chilies are a New World plant that conquered the globe. T1: chili burn is not a taste, it is CAPSAICIN, a chemical that fools the same nerve sensor that detects real hot temperature, so your mouth thinks it is literally burning. T2 (myth-buster): the capsaicin is NOT in the seeds; it is concentrated in the pale spongy PITH/placenta the seeds cling to, so that is the hottest part to cut out. T3: chili heat is rated on the SCOVILLE scale, from a bell pepper at zero up to superhots like the Carolina Reaper. T4 (accuracy/history payoff): chilies are native to the AMERICAS; there were NO chilies in India, Thailand, Sichuan, or Hungary until explorers carried them from the New World after 1492, so those cuisines' fiery reputations are less than about 500 years old. T5: capsaicin is oil-like, so WATER just spreads it, while milk (the protein casein) washes it off, which is why dairy cools a curry and water does not. T6 (evolution): birds do not feel capsaicin at all, so chilies bribe birds to eat the fruit and spread the seeds while deterring mammals that would crush them. T5: paprika is simply dried, ground sweet/mild chilies, which Hungary turned into a national spice, and smoking it makes Spanish pimenton.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Capsaicin' and 'Scoville scale', Biology Insights 'What Really Causes Peppers to Be Hot', PepperGeek 'What Makes Peppers Spicy'.
framing_note: Prep-frame welcome ('you bite the chili / you cut out the...'). Invert the wonder: big Scoville numbers are the HOOK in the stem, the answer is the mechanism/origin/plant-part. Accuracy rail (hard): chilies are NEW WORLD, no chili anywhere in Asia or Europe before Columbus, never imply ancient Indian/Thai/Sichuan chili. Second rail: heat lives in the PITH/placenta, NOT the seeds (bust the myth). Dinner-test payoff: the New-World-origin rung (T4), that Asian chili heat is only ~500 years old.

name: Cinnamon: the bark that curls
scope: Cinnamon is tree bark, and the cheap kind is not the 'true' kind. T1: cinnamon is the inner BARK of a tree, peeled in strips that curl into quills as they dry, so a cinnamon stick is a rolled tube of bark. T2: 'true' cinnamon (Ceylon, Cinnamomum verum) comes from SRI LANKA and is pale, thin, and delicate. T3 (honest fact): most cinnamon on supermarket shelves is actually CASSIA, a cheaper cousin from China/Indonesia with bolder, redder, thicker bark. T4 (honest nutrition): cassia carries far more COUMARIN, a compound hard on the liver in large daily doses, so a sprinkle is fine but Ceylon is the safer choice for someone eating a lot of it. T5 (label-the-legend): ancient traders hid cinnamon's source with a tall tale, that giant 'cinnamon birds' built cliff-nests of it, to disguise the fact that it simply came by sea from the East.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Healthline 'Ceylon vs Cassia Cinnamon', Wikipedia 'Cinnamon' and 'Cinnamomum verum', The Spice House 'Ceylon vs Cassia'. Cinnamon-bird legend traces to Herodotus (label as ancient legend).
framing_note: Scene-led (the curling quill, the spice-rack stick); answer stays on the bark/tree/origin. Accuracy rail: distinguish true Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum, Sri Lanka) from cassia (China/Indonesia), and note most 'cinnamon' sold is cassia. Handle the coumarin fact honestly WITHOUT fearmongering (normal cooking amounts are safe). Label the cinnamon-bird story clearly as ANCIENT LEGEND. Dinner-test payoff: the Ceylon-vs-cassia rung (T3).

name: Cloves: the unopened flower bud
scope: A clove is a flower that never got to bloom. T1: a whole clove is a dried FLOWER BUD, picked from the tree just BEFORE it would open; the little 'nail' shape is the closed bud with its unopened petals balled up on top. T2: cloves come from the MALUKU (Molucca) islands of Indonesia, the original Spice Islands, in the same waters as nutmeg's Bandas. T3 (amazing fact): cloves are loaded with EUGENOL, the oil behind that warm sharp smell, and it is the same numbing compound dentists have long used on a toothache. T4 (technique): because one clove is so intense, cooks use them whole (a couple studded into a ham or an onion) and fish them out, rather than dumping in ground clove.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Clove', McCormick Science Institute 'Cloves', Kew POWO 'Syzygium aromaticum' (flower buds; Maluku origin; eugenol 72-90% of oil; dental/numbing use).
framing_note: Scene-led (the nail-shaped bud, the clove-studded ham). Accuracy rail: cloves are flower BUDS picked before they open, not seeds or berries. The eugenol/dentist link is the amazing-fact payoff (T3): frame as 'why cloves numb your gums', with the answer being the clove/its oil, not the molecule name (eugenol may be context or a distractor, never the required answer). Dinner-test payoff: the dentist-numbing rung.

name: Ginger and turmeric: the underground rhizomes
scope: Two kitchen 'roots' that are not roots at all. T1: the knobby ginger you grate is not a root, it is a RHIZOME, an underground STEM that creeps sideways and sends up shoots (turmeric grows the same way). T2: turmeric is the same kind of rhizome but bright ORANGE inside, and its pigment (curcumin) is what stains everything yellow, giving most 'curry powder' its color. T3: ginger and turmeric are close cousins in the same GINGER FAMILY, along with cardamom and galangal. T4 (mechanism): fresh ginger's sharp zing comes from gingerol, and drying or cooking changes that compound, which is why dried and cooked ginger taste warmer and mellower than raw. T5 (technique): candied ginger, pickled sushi ginger, and ground baking ginger are all the SAME rhizome processed differently; heat and time, not different plants, make them taste so different.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Ginger', 'Turmeric', 'Rhizome', 'Zingiberaceae' (rhizomes are underground stems; curcumin pigment; ginger family relatives).
framing_note: Scene-led (grating the knobby 'root'). Accuracy rail (the hook): ginger and turmeric are RHIZOMES (underground stems), NOT roots; this pairs with the herb/spice backbone ladder but the payoff here is the deeper why. Turmeric = the yellow in curry (curcumin as CONTEXT, not the tested term). Dinner-test payoff: the rhizome-not-a-root rung (T1). Keep curcumin/gingerol as context/distractors, not banned-jargon answers.

name: Cardamom: the fragrant pods
scope: The third-priciest spice hides its flavor inside little pods. T1: cardamom is sold as small green PODS, and the actual spice is the sticky black SEEDS packed inside; you crush the pod to free them. T2: cardamom is a cousin of ginger (same ginger family), native to the rainforests of southern INDIA. T3 (surprise origin): the world's largest EXPORTER of cardamom today is not India but GUATEMALA, where it was planted in the twentieth century and now thrives. T4: after saffron and vanilla, cardamom is the THIRD most expensive spice by weight, because the pods are hand-harvested. T5 (culinary reach): the same pod perfumes both sweet Scandinavian buns and Middle Eastern coffee, and anchors Indian garam masala, one spice bridging very different kitchens.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Cardamom', CBI market report 'European market potential for cardamom' (Guatemala now largest exporter), NC State Extension 'Elettaria cardamomum'.
framing_note: Scene-led (splitting the green pod for the seeds). Accuracy rail: the spice is the SEEDS inside the pod (whole pods are cooked to release them); India is the native home but Guatemala is now the top exporter. Dinner-test payoff: the Guatemala-largest-exporter surprise (T3), or the pod-holds-the-seeds fact (T1). Keep 'third most expensive' as a hook, not a number to memorize.

name: Coriander, cumin and the umbel-seed family
scope: A family of seed-spices from lacy flower heads, plus one plant that is two spices at once. T1 (two-for-one wonder): cilantro (the leaf) and coriander (the seed) are the SAME plant (Coriandrum sativum); the fresh green leaf and the dried round seed taste completely different. T2 (honest fact): to some people cilantro leaves taste like SOAP, a real quirk of smell genes (a receptor tuned to the leaf's aldehydes), not fussiness. T3: cumin is a different SEED entirely, small ridged seeds toasted and ground, an ancient Egyptian spice and the earthy backbone of chili powder and many curries. T4 (accuracy/lookalike): cumin and CARAWAY look almost identical and get mixed up, but they are different plants with different flavors (cumin earthy-warm, caraway the sharper rye-bread seed). T5 (botany payoff): coriander, cumin, caraway, dill, fennel, and anise are all SEEDS of the same plant family (the umbellifers/Apiaceae), whose flowers spread like a tiny umbrella (an 'umbel').
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Coriander', 'Cumin', 'OR6A2', Flavour journal 'A genetic variant near olfactory receptor genes influences cilantro preference' (Eriksson et al.), HealthPartners 'cilantro soap gene'.
framing_note: Scene-led. Flagship rung is the one-plant-two-spices reveal (cilantro leaf = coriander seed). Accuracy rails: coriander (seed) is NOT the same as cumin (different plant, commonly confused); cumin is NOT caraway (lookalikes). Handle the cilantro-soap fact honestly as a smell-gene quirk with a SMALL real effect (it explains a tendency, not destiny). Dinner-test payoff: the cilantro=coriander same-plant rung (T1). Keep the receptor name as context, never the tested answer.

name: Toasting and blooming: why you heat whole spices
scope: The reason recipes tell you to toast or 'bloom' spices before using them. T1: a spice's smell lives in its VOLATILE OILS, aromatic compounds locked in the seed or bark that fly off as vapor when warmed, which is why a spice 'wakes up' the instant it hits a hot pan. T2 (technique): dry-TOASTING whole spices in a pan releases and deepens those aromas (with a little browning), which is why cooks toast and grind fresh instead of starting with old ground powder. T3 (mechanism): many spice flavors are FAT-SOLUBLE, so 'blooming' them in hot oil or butter pulls the flavor into the fat and spreads it through the whole dish, something water cannot do. T4 (freshness): whole spices keep their punch for months while PRE-GROUND spice fades fast, because grinding exposes all those oils to air and they oxidize away, so you grind fresh for the biggest flavor. T5 (blends): garam masala and Chinese five-spice are built by TOASTING whole spices together and then grinding; the toasting is what marries them (five-spice's showpiece is star anise, the star-shaped fruit of an Asian tree).
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via The Spice Trader 'Toasting vs Blooming Spices', CookWell 'Bloom' technique, MasalaBear 'The Science of Spice Blooming' (volatile, fat-soluble aromatic oils released by heat; oil as solvent water cannot match).
framing_note: Prep-frame IS the point ('the recipe says toast the cumin first, why?'). Answer is the mechanism (volatile oils released by heat; fat-soluble flavors bloom in oil). Accuracy rail: it is about RELEASING/transforming volatile aromatic oils (plus light browning), not 'cooking out' flavor. Dinner-test payoff: the fat-soluble blooming rung (T3), why you fry spices in oil, not water. Keep any compound names as context, not tested answers.

name: Allspice: the New World berry that tastes like three spices
scope: One berry that fooled Europeans into thinking it was a blend. T1: allspice is a single dried unripe BERRY (from the tree Pimenta dioica), and its name comes from tasting like CLOVES, CINNAMON, and NUTMEG all at once, so English cooks assumed it must be a mix. T2 (accuracy): it is NOT a spice blend, it is one berry from one tree; the 'all-spice' name is about its combined flavor, not its ingredients. T3 (origin/history): allspice is a NEW WORLD spice, met by Columbus's crews in the Caribbean, and it is essentially the only major spice still grown almost entirely in the Americas (Jamaica is the top source), and it is the defining flavor of Jamaican jerk seasoning.
source: Grokipedia blocked this session; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Allspice', Britannica 'allspice' (Pimenta dioica; dried unripe berry; named by the English c.1621 for its combined flavor; New World / Jamaica production).
framing_note: Scene-led (the peppercorn-looking berry that smells like Christmas baking). Accuracy rail (hard): allspice is ONE berry, NOT a blend of several spices, bust that near-universal assumption; and it is a NEW WORLD plant (Jamaica/Caribbean), so no allspice in the Old World before Columbus. Dinner-test payoff: the 'it's one berry, not a mix' reveal (T2).
